big_idea: Products that become habits don't rely on advertising to pull users back; they're engineered around a repeatable psychological loop that links a user's internal need to the company's product as the solution.

tool.label: The Hook Model
tool.text: A four-step cycle designed to build habitual product use: a trigger (external, like a notification, or eventually internal, like boredom) prompts an action (the simplest behavior done in anticipation of a reward); that action delivers a variable reward (unpredictable payoffs of the tribe, the hunt, or the self that keep users curious rather than satiated); and the user makes an investment (time, data, effort, or social capital) that loads the next trigger and increases the odds of returning, turning the loop into a self-reinforcing flywheel.
tool.note: Eyal pairs the model with a Manipulation Matrix that asks builders whether their product genuinely improves users' lives and whether they'd use it themselves, explicitly to flag when habit-forming design tips into manipulation.

ideas.title: Motivation + ability + trigger = behavior
ideas.text: Borrowed from BJ Fogg's behavior model, a trigger only produces action when the user is sufficiently motivated and the action is easy enough to do.

ideas.title: External vs. internal triggers
ideas.text: Early product use relies on external cues like push notifications; the goal over time is for the product to become linked to an internal cue, anxiety, boredom, FOMO, so users return unprompted.

ideas.title: Variable reward types
ideas.text: Eyal categorizes rewards into the tribe (social validation), the hunt (resources or information), and the self (mastery or competence); mixing unpredictability into any of these sustains interest longer than a fixed payoff.

ideas.title: The IKEA effect and sunk cost
ideas.text: Small user investments, adding a profile photo, following people, building a playlist, increase perceived value and make leaving the product feel like a loss.

ideas.title: Reducing friction over adding motivation
ideas.text: It's often easier and more effective to simplify the action, fewer steps, fewer decisions, than to try to boost user motivation directly.

ideas.title: Ethical responsibility of habit design
ideas.text: Because the Hook Model can build genuinely useful habits or exploitative ones, the authors argue builders have an obligation to ask who benefits from the habit being formed.

try_it: Map one feature of your own product or workflow tool against all four Hook steps and identify which step is currently weakest.
Run the Manipulation Matrix on something you're building: does it materially improve the user's life, and would you use it yourself?
Audit your own most-used app and identify its internal trigger, what emotion sends you back to it without a notification?
Reduce one step of friction from a task you want a team or customer to repeat, then observe whether completion rates change.
best_for: Product managers, designers, and founders building consumer or B2B software meant to be used repeatedly
Marketers wanting the psychology behind engagement and retention
less_useful: Readers looking for a business-model or go-to-market book, since this is specifically about behavioral product design, not pricing or strategy
Anyone uncomfortable with the ethical gray area of intentionally engineering habitual behavior
